annotations.title: What Your Resume Is Up Against
Ladders Updates Popular Recruiter Eye-Tracking Study With New Key Insights on How Job Seekers Can Improve Their Resumes
What Your Resume Is Up Against

content.text:
**Sometimes for an initial skim—but “six seconds per résumé” isn’t a universal rule.**

The claim comes from a **2012 study by the job site TheLadders**, which tracked the eye movements of **30 recruiters**. It reported roughly six seconds to make an initial “fit/no fit” decision—not necessarily the total time spent evaluating a candidate. ([forbes.com](https://www.forbes.com/sites/susanadams/2012/03/26/what-your-resume-is-up-against/?utm_source=openai))

A **2018 update reported 7.4 seconds**, again specifically for the initial screening. That’s evidence of a quick first pass, not a deadline that every recruiter follows. ([prnewswire.com](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/ladders-updates-popular-recruiter-eye-tracking-study-with-new-key-insights-on-how-job-seekers-can-improve-their-resumes-300744217.html?utm_source=openai))

There are reasons to be cautious: the original sample was small, and the research came from a commercial career-services company. It doesn’t establish how every recruiter reviews every résumé across industries and hiring situations. ([forbes.com](https://www.forbes.com/sites/susanadams/2012/03/26/what-your-resume-is-up-against/?utm_source=openai))

**My practical takeaway: make your fit easy to spot, rather than trying to make your entire résumé readable in six seconds.** I’d prioritize:
- Clear job titles, employers, and dates.
- Relevant qualifications near the top.
- Short accomplishment bullets rather than dense paragraphs.
- Enough detail to reward a closer read.

Think **“easy to skim, useful to read,”** not “six seconds or you’re out.”
